toxinNotes: Illudin S. Onset is fast — typically 30 minutes to 2 hours — with severe vomiting, cramping and diarrhea. Rarely fatal in healthy adults, but dehydration is serious and hospitalization is common. There is no antidote; treatment is supportive. The gills are genuinely bioluminescent, but the glow is faint, needs a fully dark-adapted eye and fresh material, and is not a field test.
ecologyNotes:
Saprotrophic and weakly parasitic on hardwood, overwhelmingly oak in Kentucky. Fruits in dense clusters with the stem bases fused into a common mass, on stumps, root flares and buried roots. The buried-root habit is the trap: a cluster arising from a root ten centimetres down looks like it is growing out of bare soil, so 'growing from the ground' is not the same evidence as 'mycorrhizal with soil'. True gills — thin, sharp-edged, knife-like, separable from the cap flesh. Cap and flesh orange throughout.

OPEN QUESTION FOR REVIEW: spore print recorded as 'white'; it is usually described as cream to very pale yellow. It is deliberately listed as a red herring in this confusion set because at field resolution it does not separate Omphalotus from Cantharellus — confirm that is right, because it is the pedagogical point of the set.
